objective: Provide a provider-neutral hardware capability, topology, path-selection, partitioning, and host-discovery layer that improves portability across CPU, vector, accelerator, memory, DMA, RDMA, CXL, storage, virtualization, power, and thermal environments without replacing Linux drivers or claiming unmeasured physical hardware behavior.

research.conclusion: CXL Type-3 memory is surfaced through ACPI/PCI discovery, NUMA node creation, memory tiers, DAX, and memory hotplug; driver-managed memory is kept separate from kernel update regions.
research.implementation_impact: M247 represents CXL and memory-tier facts as provider-neutral capability observations while leaving firmware, decoder, DAX, and memory-hotplug control to Linux adapters.

research.conclusion: VFIO exposes direct userspace device access through an IOMMU-protected environment; IOMMU groups are the minimum ownership/isolation unit and topology can reduce isolation granularity.
research.implementation_impact: M247 requires explicit isolation and attestation evidence for direct paths and treats IOMMU/VFIO metadata as measured constraints rather than authority.

research.conclusion: IOMMUFD provides IOAS, device, HWPT, nested translation, virtual-IOMMU, fault, and DMA-ownership objects; a device must establish DMA ownership before safe use.
research.implementation_impact: M247 includes IOMMUFD-compatible path vocabulary and fail-closed topology/path digests without implementing a replacement IOMMU or claiming DMA isolation.

research.conclusion: RDMA fast paths can use userspace-mapped hardware while slow-path resource management remains in the kernel; opaque handles, cleanup, memory pinning, and resource accounting are required.
research.implementation_impact: M247 exposes RDMA as a capability/path observation and keeps resource lifecycle and isolation explicit; no live RDMA hardware was available in this environment.

features: provider-neutral CPU, SIMD/vector, GPU, NPU, TPU, FPGA, memory, storage, network, and virtual-device classes
explicit capability vocabulary for tensor, DMA, peer DMA, RDMA, CXL, IOMMU, confidential computing, hotplug, power, thermal, asynchronous I/O, and direct userspace paths
versioned device and topology path records with identity/path digests, generation fencing, health, driver verification, attestation, isolation, bandwidth, latency, power, and thermal fields
deterministic topology-aware execution-path selection with bandwidth, latency, thermal headroom, power headroom, capability, isolation, attestation, and generation gates
explicit CPU fallback only when requested and accelerator-only isolation or attestation requirements are deliberately relaxed
partition reservation and release with memory/compute accounting, grant digest, generation fencing, double-release protection, and tamper rejection
observation-only host discovery from procfs/sysfs for CPU count, vector features, memory, DRM, RDMA, NVMe, CXL, power, thermal, and TPM device presence
canonical path and discovery digests with fail-closed malformed or tampered metadata admission
provider-neutral vocabulary compatible with Linux VFIO/IOMMUFD/RDMA/CXL adapters without replacing upstream driver mechanisms

discovery.interpretation: These are observations from the current sandbox procfs/sysfs environment. Zero device counts mean no visible devices were observed, not that the platform lacks support. No physical accelerator or root-of-trust qualification is claimed.

benchmark.interpretation: The selection path includes mutex synchronization, device and path filtering, topology checks, deterministic scoring, and SHA-256 decision binding. The static loop is an in-memory predicate and is not apples-to-apples; this is a capability-selection overhead baseline, not an accelerator-throughput or end-to-end latency superiority claim.

qualification_limits: M247 is a userspace/reference hardware capability and path-selection layer; it does not replace Linux CPU, GPU, NPU, RDMA, NVMe, CXL, VFIO, IOMMUFD, KVM, container, or power-management drivers.

Host discovery reports only the current procfs/sysfs environment and cannot establish device performance, firmware correctness, isolation granularity, DMA behavior, thermal behavior, or power efficiency.
No physical GPU, NPU, TPU, FPGA, HBM/VRAM, IOMMU, DMA, RDMA, CXL, NVMe, confidential-computing, or vendor-driver qualification was possible in this sandbox.

The 1202.47 ns/request selection result is a local userspace decision overhead baseline and must not be presented as an inference-latency, tokens-per-second, accelerator-utilization, or energy-per-inference claim.

QEMU validates only the tested virtualized boot and soak profiles. It does not qualify physical hardware, hotplug, PCIe topology, firmware, power, thermal, accelerator reset, or live multihost behavior.

Production release remains blocked by independent builder equivalence, operator signing and trusted-key lifecycle, physical accelerator and IOMMU/DMA qualification, live RDMA/CXL/NVMe qualification, independent external security review, production PKI/KMS/TPM attestation, live migration and rollback, and operator-owned CVE response.
